title: New Study Confirms a Core Truth About Learning
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick uses a new study of 108 German third-graders learning spelling rules to reaffirm a counterintuitive principle of learning science: making practice harder in the short term often produces better long-term learning. He first explains interleaving as fundamentally about discrimination, forcing learners to distinguish between problem types, and notes its built-in retrieval benefit. The study found interleaved practice produced more errors and felt harder but yielded fewer spelling errors at posttest and eight-week follow-up, mainly for students with average to high prior knowledge. Hendrick then draws his own inference: because similar spelling rules invite confusion under blocked practice, and spelling depends on morphology rather than sounding out, the findings strengthen the case for explicit instruction before interleaved practice. He weighs the study's limitations, including teacher contamination and a short intervention, against its preregistered design. He closes by arguing the result shows science-of-learning principles transcend maths and science to literacy.
points: Hendrick frames interleaving as a discrimination task: encountering different items back-to-back forces learners to notice what distinguishes one rule or problem type from another.
Interleaving is described as having a 'built-in superpower' of forced retrieval, because items do not repeat and short-term memory cannot carry the learner.
The benefits appeared mainly in students with average to high prior spelling knowledge, which Hendrick uses to argue for explicit instruction in the rules first.
He treats the study as credible despite 35% of teachers covering target rules before follow-up, citing preregistration, controls, counterbalancing and the eight-week follow-up.
The practical advice includes warning students that interleaving will feel harder and judging progress by long-term retention rather than ease during practice.
quotes: Interleaving is essentially about discrimination. When learners encounter different items back-to-back, they must pay attention to what distinguishes one from the next. This strengthens their ability to categorize and apply the right rule or strategy.

Another important point about interleaving is its built-in superpower: it forces retrieval. Because the same item doesn't appear multiple times in a row, students can't rely on short-term memory. They have to retrieve the rule or pattern afresh, which boosts long-term retention.

While students made more errors during interleaved practice and perceived it as more difficult, they showed superior performance on both trained and untrained words at immediate posttest and 8-week follow-up. Notably, these benefits were primarily observed in students with average to high prior spelling knowledge.

The implication here is that traditional blocked practice may inadvertently amplify confusion. Because the rules are so alike, practicing them in isolation doesn't give learners enough contrast to spot the unique features of each rule.

The authors suggest that the lack of short-term transfer effects in their study may be due to the cognitive complexity of spelling rules, which require time and repeated exposure to consolidate. In other words, interleaving supports deeper learning, but its full benefits (especially for generalization) take time to surface.

There are some limitations to this study that are important to consider. First, 35% of teachers covered the target spelling rules between posttest and follow-up despite instructions not to, potentially contaminating the long-term results.

The science of learning often gets criticized for only working with math and science, but this study on literacy demonstrates the broader applicability of these principles. The findings remind us that effective learning strategies transcend subject boundaries.
